name: Hana Olsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We don't sell anything or campaign, and your answers are confidential. What does an ordinary working day look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Hana, fifty-eight, a junior doing electrical preparation and simple fittings in homes and small businesses. I came in after years packing spectacles in a workshop, when that employer closed; I've a vocational certificate, not an electrician's licence. The qualified electrician shows, permits and checks my work, and I'm still below the usual standard for the job. Yesterday my conduit bend was so poor I kept the offcut to practise measuring, rather than hide it in the scrap.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is the situation at home, and how do you approach new tools?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Noah is a school caretaker; our children are grown and live elsewhere, and our small home is paid for. I get higher pay than many people in this job because this firm pays well for its awkward repair rota, and we've twenty-one months of expenses saved, with plenty of other electrical firms nearby. I use AI study questions every day, then check the answers against the course book or a qualified colleague; I like finding out, but a clever answer doesn't give me permission to touch a circuit. We see retirement ahead without knowing an affordable date, and I'd rather have people teach a useful skill than sell another grand promise.

I want **ordinary standards** to matter without needing a dramatic technology story.
think: Our **work and money** feel secure with covering wages, a paid home and twenty-one months saved.
Being a **slow beginner** is a learning problem, not an immediate household income crisis.
do: Keep **offered junior repairs** within ability, with qualified permission and checks, now and through the first year.
Continue **checked daily study** and agreed bench exercises while maintaining usual household spending.
feel: **Calm and useful**, with time to ask again rather than conceal a practical mistake.
S0.quote: A neat answer on my phone can't straighten the bend in my hand.
fieldNote: Her **strong cushion** combines higher pay, covering household wages, a paid home and twenty-one months saved rather than an assumed retirement payment.
Her **daily AI study** remains existing checked practice; it neither supplies an electrician's licence nor removes qualified permission and practical checks.

steps.text: Keep offered junior repairs within ability, permitted and checked by the qualified electrician

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the ordinary repair still deserves an ordinary standard. Keep the small time savers if they work, and let somebody show me again where my measurement went wrong. I don't need a revolution to make a straight bend worth doing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our work and money would feel secure. Both wages cover our costs comfortably, the house is paid for and twenty-one months saved is a real cushion. I'd still be the beginner with the crooked offcut, but that doesn't make the next grocery bill uncertain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the offered junior repair tasks now and through the first year, only within my ability and with the qualified electrician's permission and checks. I'd keep the daily checked study questions and practise the normal bench exercises during work as agreed. Noah and I would carry on with our usual household spending rather than invent a new purchase because the technology story was quiet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and rather pleased to have room to learn properly. I like being useful, even when useful means asking for the measurement a second time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the bend that went wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the offcut to the bench and ask the electrician to watch the point where I marked it. A neat answer on my phone can't straighten the bend in my hand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would this make retirement a settled decision?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I haven't verified our future income or what our later costs might be. Having a paid home and money saved lets us ask without rushing, not put an unearned payment into the budget.

say: I'd welcome **accurate ordering** while asking for a person to teach the practical task.
I'd seek **two bench sessions** instead of treating an app explanation as hands-on instruction.
think: My **junior hours could shrink** if experienced workers cover more visits with fewer helpers.
Our **reserve protects bills**, while neither replacing my wage permanently nor guaranteeing Noah's employment choices.
do: Book **two ninety-minute sessions** in conduit bending only with confirmed places and employer-funded materials.
Attend in **paid shifts**, protecting normal weekly wages and hours and retaining qualified supervision throughout.
Keep **offered junior tasks** during the first year only within ability, with qualified permission and checks.
feel: **Anxious but willing**, with resources to respond carefully rather than resign in a hurry.
S1.quote: I won't pay the firm for the time the firm needs me to learn.
fieldNote: Her **anxiety follows hours**, despite enough savings to prevent an immediate bill crisis; the reserve does not make lost earnings irrelevant.
Her **specific training choice** needs confirmed sessions, employer materials and protected paid shifts, while remaining inside junior ability and qualified supervision.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say faster ordering is welcome if the right part arrives, but a beginner still needs somebody beside the bench. I'd ask for two proper conduit-bending sessions instead of being told the app has explained everything. Teaching is work too, and the firm ought to make room for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My hours could shrink if quicker planning lets experienced workers cover visits with fewer junior helpers. The reserve would let us absorb a reduction without missing bills, but I wouldn't call that the same as keeping my wage. Noah's caretaker work looks less directly exposed to thinking software, though I can't guarantee his employer's choices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd book two ninety-minute conduit-bending sessions only with confirmed places and employer-funded materials. I'd attend during paid shifts with normal weekly wages and hours protected, keeping qualified supervision throughout. During the first year I'd continue offered junior tasks only within my ability, permitted and checked by the qualified electrician.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about possibly losing hours, while quite ready to try the learning. I can afford a considered response rather than a rushed resignation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the sessions meant losing part of your normal weekly wage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd keep the usual supervised work and ask for a paid arrangement at the next work meeting. I won't pay the firm for the time the firm needs me to learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would two sessions make you an independent electrician?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I'd be practising one thing I currently do badly. I'd still need the qualified electrician to permit and check the task, and I'd still have only my vocational certificate.

I'd treat **nearby firms** as possible conversations, not positions already held in reserve.
think: My **junior wage could shrink** before robots arrive, even with a long savings cushion.
Noah's **physical work** also faces later machines, with neither employer's actual purchases known.
do: Request **income and eligibility records** with Noah and free community reading help only if available.
Review **verified income and essentials** quarterly, sooner after either wage changes, counting no unconfirmed payments.
Keep **2029 paid junior tasks** only if offered, within ability and qualified permission and checks; defer unaffordable exit.
feel: **Anxious without feeling cornered**, using the reserve to check actual choices instead of assuming a replacement wage.
S2.quote: Sixty-three is an age, not a standing order into our bank account.
fieldNote: Her **family outlook** produces a requirement to agree any offered help, rather than an entitlement to grown children's wages or labour.
Her **fast-timeline response** checks actual income and essential costs without assuming a retirement payment, robot purchase or safe future junior role.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking work changes in 2028 when I'll be sixty, with hands-on robots around 2031 when I'll be sixty-three. I'd want the firm to explain the paid junior work it actually expects between those dates. Plenty of local firms gives me places to ask questions, not a reserved position at each one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could lose junior hours before the robots, if the firm reorganises its visits. We could cover a long interruption from savings, but two adults cannot live on the same pot indefinitely. Noah's hands-on work faces later machines too, and I don't know which actual tasks either employer would buy machines for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now Noah and I would request our actual retirement-income and eligibility records and ask our community advice desk for free help reading them, only if available. We'd compare verified income and essential costs each quarter, sooner after either wage changes, counting no promised payment before confirmation. During 2029 I'd keep paid junior tasks only if offered, within ability and with qualified permission and checks; any exit would wait for an actually affordable budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about our wages, without feeling cornered. The reserve buys time to find the real answer, and I don't want to waste that time guessing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would reaching sixty-three settle the decision about work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still check whether the income covered our needs and whether either of us wanted or needed suitable work. Sixty-three is an age, not a standing order into our bank account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your grown children be part of the income plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk about practical help only if a child offered and we agreed what was affordable for them. I wouldn't count a child's income because family matters to me; family matters enough to ask first.

I'd distinguish **sixty-three and sixty-six** without promising protection for younger workers' whole careers.
think: Our **near-term finances look secure** with covering wages, a paid home and the existing reserve.
I'm **uneasy about later needs**, capacity and whether any suitable employment will actually be offered.

Seek **available free record help**; review verified income and essentials yearly, sooner after wage or health changes; assess 2032 capacity and affordability.
feel: **Uneasy about later years**, with enough present security to concentrate on useful learning now.
S3.quote: Learning today isn't a contract with my body ten years from now.
fieldNote: Her **present security** is explicit rather than inferred from extra preparation time; the later income, capacity and employment question remains open.
Her **paid bench learning** remains conditional and supervised, while the household review uses verified figures without granting a pension or funded exit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years lets me put the teaching and the household papers in order while the present wage is still coming in. Thinking AI arrives in 2031 when I'm sixty-three, then robots around 2034 at sixty-six. I wouldn't tell a younger worker that my longer preparation somehow protects their whole career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The next few years look secure for us, with covering wages, a paid home and the reserve. I'm uneasy about the later trade and what we will actually need at sixty-three or sixty-six, rather than expecting the present income to disappear immediately. I don't know our future capacity or whether any particular firm would offer us work then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the two ninety-minute conduit-bending sessions now only with confirmed places, employer-funded materials, paid shifts and normal weekly wages and hours protected, keeping qualified supervision. We'd request missing income records and available free community reading help, then review verified income and essentials with Noah yearly, sooner after a wage or health change. During 2032 we'd compare actual resources and capacity before deciding about an exit or any offered suitable paid work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the later question, but able to concentrate on the bend in front of me. I don't need to turn a useful lesson today into a promise of employment at sixty-six.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does learning now mean committing to stay in physical work later?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I'd be learning because I have a real paid task now and want to do it properly. Learning today isn't a contract with my body ten years from now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with an unclear income record?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the actual provider to explain or correct a missing entry, and use only confirmed figures meanwhile. I'd rather have an awkward blank on the page than a comfortable invented number.

I'd prefer **honest figures** to a reassuring family speech about an unchecked future.
think: Our **current work and money** look secure, with later income and physical capacity still unknown.
I cannot count **future local employment** or retirement payments from the firms and savings visible today.

feel: **Uneasy but presently secure**, checking later needs without giving away ordinary time with family now.
S4.quote: A nearby job advertisement today isn't a wage at seventy-one.
fieldNote: Her **long preparation** does not produce an assumed retirement right, affordable exit, lasting physical capacity or guaranteed job at a later age.
Her **strong resources** explain near-term security, while future family help remains voluntary and agreed rather than silently included as income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I would be sixty-eight at the thinking change in 2036 and seventy-one when robots follow around 2039. Ten years gives us a chance to check the real household choices, not a licence to ignore them. I'd rather hand the family an honest page of figures than a cheerful speech.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our current work and money look secure, and I'd be thinking about later arrangements even without AI. The unsettled bit is what income and physical capacity we'll actually have then. I don't assume a retirement payment or that one of the many firms nearby now will employ me at sixty-eight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the same two ninety-minute conduit-bending sessions now only with confirmed places and employer-funded materials, during paid shifts with normal weekly wages and hours protected and qualified supervision. Noah and I would request missing income records and available free community reading help, reviewing verified income and essentials yearly, sooner after a wage or health change. During 2037 we'd check confirmed resources and actual capacity before deciding whether an exit was affordable or offered suitable paid work was needed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about making the later figures add up, but secure enough to enjoy the present. The long warning helps me ask earlier; it doesn't give me an answer I haven't earned by checking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the local employers guarantee an option when robots arrive?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, what is close by now may not exist then, and I don't know what work my body could safely do. A nearby job advertisement today isn't a wage at seventy-one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would family support be automatic at that point?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Any help would have to be chosen and agreed, with their own needs heard too. I want our children to visit because they want to, not because I've written their earnings into a table.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because junior hours could shrink before we've checked an actual next income, and Noah's physical work isn't outside the later robot picture. Protected paid teaching and help reading our real income records would be useful. Our reserve gives us time to act sensibly, not a replacement wage for the rest of our lives.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could ask whether being older makes it easier to admit you're a beginner. Some mornings yes, some mornings I want to hide the bad bend under my coat. My age doesn't give my hands the training they missed.

headlineQuote: My age doesn't give my hands the training they missed.
portrait: Hana is **fifty-eight**, a junior with a vocational certificate only, still needing qualified permission, checks and practical teaching.
Her **higher pay** and Noah's caretaker wage cover costs, with a paid home, twenty-one months saved and plenty of nearby firms.
She uses **AI study questions daily**, but values apprenticeship and accepts no licence or independent competence from a fluent explanation.
She chooses **conditional paid bench learning** and verified income reviews, retaining voluntary family help and uncertainty about later work or affordable retirement.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could shrink junior hours before a next income is verified, with Noah's physical work exposed to later robots.
whatWouldHelp: Provide **protected paid teaching** and available free help reading actual income and eligibility records, without promising a replacement wage.
